subject: Chemistry
description: Atomic radius, ionisation energy, electronegativity, electron affinity

questions.stem: ATOMIC RADIUS GENERALLY ___ as we move from LEFT TO RIGHT in a period.
questions.explanation: Across a PERIOD: nuclear charge INCREASES (more protons); electrons added to SAME shell. So nucleus pulls electrons CLOSER → atomic radius DECREASES. Across PERIOD 2: Li(152 pm) → Be(112) → B(85) → C(77) → N(75) → O(73) → F(72) → Ne(71). Li largest, F smallest. DOWN A GROUP: more shells added → radius INCREASES. So in periodic table, BOTTOM-LEFT = LARGEST atoms (Cs, Fr); TOP-RIGHT = SMALLEST (He, F). NOTE: NOBLE GASES not always given radii (no covalent bond to define); use VAN DER WAALS radius. INSIGHT — atomic size is fundamental to chemistry: smaller atoms hold electrons tighter → higher ionisation energy + electronegativity (also period trends).

questions.stem: IONISATION ENERGY ___ across a period (LEFT to RIGHT).

options.option_text: Stays the same throughout period alone

questions.explanation: IONISATION ENERGY (IE) = energy to remove outermost electron from gaseous atom. ACROSS PERIOD: smaller radius + higher Z_eff → tighter hold → IE INCREASES. DOWN GROUP: larger radius + shielding → easier to remove → IE DECREASES. Highest IE: HELIUM (2372 kJ/mol). Lowest IE: CESIUM/Fr (~376 kJ/mol). Group 1 (alkali metals) — easily lose 1e⁻ → low IE → highly reactive. Group 18 (noble gases) — highest IE in period → inert. SECOND IE > FIRST IE (already + ion holds tighter). HUGE JUMPS in successive IE indicate stable inner shells. EXAM PYQ: Mg's IE2 < IE3 by huge margin (after removing 2 valence electrons, next is from inner shell = much harder).
questions.subject: Chemistry

questions.explanation: FLUORINE — 3.98 on Pauling scale (highest). Top of Group 17 (HALOGENS). Top 4 EN: F (3.98), O (3.44), Cl (3.16), N (3.04). Cesium, Francium = least EN (~0.7-0.8). EN INCREASES across period (atoms smaller + more electron-greedy); DECREASES down group. INSIGHT — EN explains BOND TYPES: ΔEN ~0 → covalent (e.g., O-O, H-H); 0.5-1.7 → polar covalent (e.g., H-F, H-O — water dipole); >1.7 → ionic (Na-F, Li-Cl). HF — strongest H-bond donor; HF is also weak acid (despite F's huge EN). FLUORINE — extremely reactive, only NOBLE GAS that reacts with F is XENON. Used in: F-containing pharmaceuticals (~30% of new drugs), Teflon, refrigerants, toothpaste fluoride.

questions.stem: MENDELEEV (1869) arranged elements in order of:

options.option_text: Atomic mass (later corrected to atomic number)
Density of the element alone (option here)
Discovery year of the element (option here)

questions.explanation: MENDELEEV (Russian, 1869) — published periodic table in order of ATOMIC MASS. LEFT GAPS for undiscovered elements (e.g., predicted properties of 'eka-aluminium' = Gallium, 'eka-silicon' = Germanium, 'eka-boron' = Scandium — all later discovered with predicted properties → vindicated his table). PROBLEM: some pairs were 'misordered' by mass (e.g., Te-I, Ar-K, Co-Ni). MOSELEY (1913, English) — discovered ATOMIC NUMBER (= proton count) is the TRUE ordering principle. Modern table uses ATOMIC NUMBER. Mendeleev's contribution still recognised: 'Mendeleev's Periodic Law'; element 101 named MENDELEVIUM. INDIAN scientists' role: not in original table; KMSh Sankuriah, modern Indian periodic-table research at IISc, BARC.

questions.stem: Modern PERIODIC TABLE has how many GROUPS?
questions.explanation: Modern Periodic Table: 18 GROUPS (vertical columns), 7 PERIODS (horizontal rows). 118 confirmed elements (heaviest = Oganesson, Og, atomic # 118). GROUP NAMES: 1 (alkali metals), 2 (alkaline earth metals), 3-12 (transition metals), 13 (boron family), 14 (carbon family), 15 (nitrogen / pnictogens), 16 (chalcogens), 17 (halogens), 18 (noble gases). LANTHANIDES (57-71) + ACTINIDES (89-103) shown separately at bottom. METALS (left + middle) ~75% of elements; NON-METALS (right); METALLOIDS (zigzag border — B, Si, Ge, As, Sb, Te, Po). SUPERHEAVY ELEMENTS (Z > 104, transactinides) — synthetic, mostly very short-lived. Period 8 may add elements 119+ in future (research ongoing).
questions.subject: Chemistry

questions.explanation: ALKALI METALS (Li, Na, K, Rb, Cs, Fr) — extremely REACTIVE; rapidly oxidise in air, react VIOLENTLY with water (2Na + 2H₂O → 2NaOH + H₂↑ + heat → can ignite H₂). STORED under KEROSENE / paraffin oil to prevent contact with air + moisture. Cesium ignites SPONTANEOUSLY in air. Reactivity INCREASES down group: Li (calm) → Na (vigorous) → K (purple flame) → Rb, Cs (explosive). FLAME COLOURS (PYQ): Li (crimson), Na (yellow), K (lilac), Rb (red-violet), Cs (blue). USES: Li-ion batteries (smartphones, EVs); Na in lights, Na-K coolant in some reactors; K essential for plants + animals (potassium ions); Cs in atomic clocks. NEVER touch alkali metals with bare hands (skin moisture + warmth can ignite Na, K immediately).

questions.stem: NOBLE GASES (Group 18) are CHEMICALLY INERT because:

options.option_text: They have stable, FILLED outer electron shells
They are too small to react with anything
They are radioactive and avoid bonding

questions.explanation: NOBLE GASES (He, Ne, Ar, Kr, Xe, Rn, Og) — outer shell FULL (8 e⁻ for all except He which has 2). 'OCTET RULE' — atoms tend to acquire 8 valence electrons → noble-gas configurations are most stable. So noble gases don't NEED to gain/lose/share electrons → no chemical reactivity. EXCEPTIONS — heavier ones (Kr, Xe, Rn) form some compounds with F, O (XeF₂, XeF₄, XeF₆ — first noble gas compound: XePtF₆, Bartlett 1962). USES: HELIUM (party balloons; cooling MRI; airships), NEON (signs); ARGON (inert atmosphere for welding, light bulbs); KRYPTON (high-end car headlamps); XENON (flash lamps, anaesthetic). RADON — radioactive, accumulates in basements; cancer risk. OGANESSON — heaviest, theoretical, very short-lived. Indian: He critical for ISRO + science; mostly imported.
